Dismissive

/diss-MISS-iv/ - the stress falls on MISS · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Dismissive means treating something as unworthy of serious attention.

One dismissive glance at the demo — 'toys,' the buyer said — and he moved on to the next booth.

Worked Example

When the apprentice glassblower floated the idea of selling the workshop's misfired pieces as seconds, the master answered without looking up: 'We don't sell mistakes.' No questions, no glance at the samples she had carried in — the idea was waved off before it finished leaving her mouth.

Dismissive is the exact word because it names treatment, not just mood: the idea was treated as unworthy of serious attention — no weighing, no questions, just the brush-off. A doubting master would have examined the samples first and then said no. The dismissive one refuses the examining itself; the wave of the hand does all the arguing.

How Dismissive Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

offhand

offhand: brisk and unconsidered — without the ruling that a thing is beneath attention

contemptuous

contemptuous: openly scornful — the dismissive wave hardened into disrespect

Antonyms

attentive

attentive: giving something careful notice

receptive

receptive: open to what is being offered

How Strong Is It? — unconvinced → dismissive → contemptuous

unconvinced vs. dismissive

unconvinced vs. dismissive: An unconvinced listener has weighed the case and still doubts it; a dismissive one won't put it on the scale at all.

contemptuous vs. dismissive

contemptuous vs. dismissive: Contemptuous goes past dismissive: the dismissive editor waves the manuscript away, while the contemptuous one makes sure you see what she thinks of you for sending it.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — dis-

Prefix — dis-: away

Root — miss

Root — miss: to send

Suffix — -ive

Suffix — -ive: tending to

Put it together

Put it together: Dis- (away) + miss (to send, from Latin mittere) + -ive (tending to) = tending to send away. To dismiss is literally to send off — a class, a case, a servant — and a dismissive manner performs the same act on ideas: it sends them away unheard.

Word Choice

neutral / judging

Dismissive describes how someone treats a thing — as unworthy of a hearing. It pairs off with two unit-mates: disdain is the feeling of looking down, dismissive is that feeling in action, and disregard is what follows — the looking away itself. A dismissive reply takes two seconds; its cost is whatever the unheard idea was worth.
